newsitem.title: UK: Belfast bomb fans fears of tit-for-tat violence.
newsitem.headline: Belfast bomb fans fears of tit-for-tat violence.

text.p: A Roman Catholic man was injured on Sunday when a bomb exploded under his car in a nationalist area of north Belfast, fanning fears that Northern Ireland could be on the brink of a new cycle of sectarian violence.

Eddie Copeland, 25, a well-known republican, was taken to hospital with serious leg injuries after what a senior police officer said had been "a localised explosion", possibly beneath the driver's seat of the car.

"The windows were blown out in houses next door," Bobby Lavery, a local councillor for Sinn Fein, the political wing of the Irish Republican Army, told reporters as British troops and armed police stood guard by the damaged car in the Ardoyne district, a nationalist stronghold.

No one immediately claimed responsibility for the blast, which occurred less than 48 hours after the IRA admitted shooting a policeman guarding a prominent pro-British Protestant politician as he visited his sick son in a children's hospital.
Joe Hendron, a Belfast member of parliament for the moderate nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party, said the booby-trapped bomb appeared to be a reprisal for Friday's shooting.
Hendron said he was alarmed. "The big worry at the moment for all of us is whether what's happened today is the beginning of a tit-for-tat (round of violence)," he told BBC radio.
"All of these events put massive pressure on the republican leadership to call a credible ceasefire," Hendron added.
Ian Paisley Jr, a spokesman for the hardline Protestant Democratic Unionist Party led by his namesake father, said the bombing might well have been a retaliatory attack by Loyalist extremists.
"If it is, I utterly condemn it and say it is wrong and not the way to resolve this problem in Northern Ireland," Paisley Jr told BBC radio.
Friday's attack was the first shooting by the IRA, which wants to oust Britain from Northern Ireland, since the guerrillas ended a 17-month truce last February.
The shooting immediately sparked fears that the IRA's extremist Protestant foes, who want Northern Ireland to remain British, would call off their own two-year-old ceasefire.
David Ervine, a leader of the political arm of the outlawed Ulster Volunteer Force, said he was deeply unhappy about Sunday's blast. "I think it is potentially the beginning of a spiral," he said.
